Section 143A allows trial courts to award up to 20% interim compensation within 60 days.
Section 148 empowers appellate courts to demand a minimum 20% deposit of compensation during appeals.
Surinder Singh Deswal established that the appellate deposit under Section 148 is mandatory in the absence of exceptional circumstances.
Jamboo Bhandari requires appellate courts to record brief reasons and consider exceptional hardship before ordering deposits.
Unpaid interim compensation or deposits are recoverable as fines under the CrPC.
21.importance_reason: This is a high-yield, contemporary amendment topic that frequently appears in exams because it represents the most significant structural overhaul of modern cheque bounce litigation in India.

22.topic: Role and duties of the paying banker
22.lecture_title: Role and Duties of the Paying Banker under the Negotiable Instruments Act
22.memory_hook: Think of the paying banker as a strict nightclub bouncer at a VIP party: they must check the ID (signature and material integrity) of every guest at the door, but they are not required to search the guests' pockets for stolen cash (underlying commercial disputes).
22.concept_explanation:
When a customer opens a current or savings account with a commercial bank, a debtor-creditor relationship is established, coupled with a contractual obligation on the banker to honour the customer's cheques up to the amount of the credit balance or agreed overdraft. The banker who pays a cheque drawn by their customer is known as the 'paying banker'. Because the paying banker handles the customer's funds, this role comes with profound fiduciary responsibilities and strict legal duties. The primary duty is to obey the mandate of the customer implicitly, provided the instructions are clear, unambiguous, and lawful.

Fulfilling this duty is a tightrope walk for the banker. On one hand, if the banker wrongfully dishonours a customer's valid cheque, they face severe liability for damages to the customer's business reputation and creditworthiness. On the other hand, if the banker pays a cheque that is forged, materially altered, or presented without a proper endorsement, they generally cannot debit the customer's account and must bear the loss themselves. To mitigate this harsh common law liability, the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and the Reserve Bank of India framework provide statutory protection to paying bankers who act in 'due course' and without negligence.

The duties of a paying banker can be broadly divided into statutory obligations, contractual duties, and precautionary measures. Statutory duties include verifying the apparent tenor of the instrument, ensuring there are no legal bars to payment (such as a garnishee order or notice of the customer's death, insolvency, or insanity), and making payment within banking hours. Contractual duties stem from the implied contract of mandate between the banker and customer. Precautionary measures require the banker to exercise reasonable care and skill in detecting forgeries, material alterations, and missing or irregular endorsements.

Ultimately, the paying banker's operational safety relies heavily on statutory immunities like Section 85 and Section 128 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. These provisions protect the banker when they make payments in due course on bearer cheques or crossed cheques, respectively. However, these immunities are conditional upon the banker acting in good faith and without negligence. If the banker misses an obvious red flag, the protection vanishes, and the bank must absorb the financial blow.
key_provisions: Section 10 — Defines 'Holder in Due Course' and sets the standard for acting in good faith and without negligence.
Section 31 — Imposes statutory liability on the drawee banker for wrongful dishonour of a customer's cheque without sufficient funds or valid excuse.
Section 85 — Protects the paying banker when making payment on order cheques bearing a regular endorsement in due course.
Section 85(2) — Protects the banker when paying bearer cheques, regardless of any subsequent endorsement.
Section 89 — Protects the paying banker against material alterations if the alteration is not apparent upon reasonable inspection.
Section 128 — Protects the banker who makes payment on a crossed cheque in accordance with the crossing.

case_laws.case_name: London Joint Stock Bank Ltd. v. Macmillan
case_laws.facts: A firm's partner signed a blank cheque form and handed it to a confidential clerk to fill in the amount for petty cash. The clerk filled in the words 'two pounds' and the figures '£2', but left spaces that allowed him to add 'one hundred' and '£120' respectively. The bank paid £120 and debited the firm's account.
case_laws.holding: The House of Lords held that the customer owes a duty of care to the banker in drawing the cheque so as not to facilitate fraud or material alteration. Since the customer acted negligently by leaving spaces, the loss fell on the customer.
case_laws.why_it_matters: Established the foundational principle that a customer's negligence in drawing a negotiable instrument can preclude them from holding the paying banker liable for paying an altered amount.

case_laws.case_name: Bligh v. National Bank of India
case_laws.facts: A bank paid a cheque after receiving explicit notice from the customer that the chequebook had been lost and instructing the bank not to make any payments on it. Despite this notice, the teller paid out funds due to a failure in operational verification.
case_laws.holding: The court held that once a countermand of payment (stop-payment order) is received by the bank, the banker's mandate to pay is revoked. Paying thereafter renders the bank entirely liable.
case_laws.why_it_matters: Reinforces the absolute nature of a customer's countermand of payment and strips the banker of statutory protection if they ignore stop notices.

case_laws.case_name: Commrs. of State Savings Bank v. Permewan Wright & Co.
case_laws.facts: A company's employee fraudulently obtained signatures on cheques and endorsed them using rubber stamps or irregular signatures, which the paying bank processed without flagging the abnormalities.
case_laws.holding: The court ruled that an endorsement is not 'regular' if it contains obvious discrepancies or lacks the proper authority apparent on its face, disallowing statutory protection under Section 85.
case_laws.why_it_matters: Clarifies the exact threshold of 'regular endorsement' and mandates that bank tellers must closely inspect endorsements on order instruments.

22.real_world_example: In a recent banking fraud case reported in Mumbai, an accounts executive of a mid-sized trading firm intercepted physical cheques signed by the directors, altered the payee names to fictitious accounts controlled by him, and deposited them across multiple bank branches. Because the alterations were crudely made and the signatures showed minor discrepancies that the paying bank's automated systems and manual tellers failed to catch, the bank initially debited the firm's account. The firm sued the bank for breach of mandate. The courts examined whether the bank exercised 'reasonable care and skill' under Section 89, highlighting how digital and physical processing gaps can destroy statutory immunities for paying banks.
22.illustration: Customer A issues a cheque for ₹50,000 to Supplier B. The cheque is stolen en route by X, who alters the amount to ₹5,050,000 by cleverly inserting digits, and changes the payee name to himself. X presents the cheque over the counter at the drawee bank. The bank teller glances at the signature, which matches the specimen, but fails to notice the subtle crowding of digits and ink shade differences indicating a material alteration. The bank pays X the full ₹5,050,000. When Customer A's statement arrives, A objects. Result: The bank cannot debit A's account for the altered amount because the alteration was apparent upon reasonable inspection, meaning the bank failed its duty of care and cannot claim the shelter of Section 89.
22.quick_answer: The paying banker is bound by contract and statutory duty to honour a customer's cheque, provided there are sufficient funds, the mandate is clear, and no legal bar exists (Section 31). The primary duties of a paying banker include: (1) verifying the customer's signature, (2) ensuring the instrument has no apparent material alterations (Section 89), (3) verifying that endorsements on order cheques are regular (Section 85), (4) respecting stop-payment orders (countermand), and (5) confirming that no statutory bars like garnishee orders, customer death, or insolvency have occurred. If a banker pays a forged or materially altered cheque through negligence, they cannot debit the customer's account and must bear the loss. Conversely, statutory immunities protect the banker when they make payments in 'due course' without negligence.
22.essay_answer:
Introduction: The relationship between a banker and customer is fundamentally contractual, giving rise to reciprocal rights and obligations. Among the most critical functions of a commercial bank is acting as a 'paying banker'—honouring the cheques drawn by its customers. While the primary duty of the banker is to obey the customer's mandate, this task involves navigating a complex landscape of legal liabilities, statutory protections, and operational duties. A failure in this duty can expose the bank to severe financial loss and litigation.

Nature of the Banker-Customer Relationship and the Duty to Pay: At the heart of the paying banker's role is the implied contract arising from Section 31 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The banker is mandated to pay cheques drawn by the customer so long as the customer maintains a sufficient credit balance or an agreed overdraft facility. This duty is not absolute; it is contingent upon the presentation of a valid instrument within banking hours at the correct branch. If a banker wrongfully dishonours a valid cheque, Section 31 renders the bank liable to compensate the customer for any loss or damage proximately caused, particularly injury to commercial reputation.

Core Duties and Precautionary Obligations: To protect both the customer's funds and the bank's capital, the paying banker must observe several strict duties:
1. Verification of Signature: The banker must verify the drawer's signature against the specimen signature card. Payment on a forged signature is a nullity; the bank cannot debit the customer's account (Welch v. Bank of England principles).
2. Inspection for Material Alterations: Under Section 89, the banker must ensure the cheque is free from apparent material alterations. If an alteration is visible to the naked eye upon reasonable inspection, paying the instrument makes the bank liable.
3. Checking Endorsements: For order cheques, the banker must ensure that endorsements are regular in sequence and form under Section 85.
4. Honouring Countermands: A customer has an absolute right to stop payment on a cheque before it is paid. Receipt of a valid stop-payment order instantly revokes the banker's authority.
5. Noting Legal Bars: The banker must halt payments upon receiving notice of the customer's death, insanity, insolvency, or upon service of a garnishee order from a court.

Statutory Immunities and Defences: Recognizing that absolute liability would paralyze banking operations, the Legislature enacted protective provisions. Section 85 protects the banker paying order cheques with regular endorsements in due course. Section 128 protects the banker paying crossed cheques according to the crossing. However, these immunities are conditional: the banker must act in good faith and without negligence. As illustrated in cases like London Joint Stock Bank v. Macmillan, if the customer's negligence contributes to the fraud, or if the bank fails to exercise reasonable care, the immunities do not apply, shifting liability back to the negligent party.

Conclusion: The role of the paying banker demands eternal vigilance. Balancing the commercial imperative of rapid customer service with the rigorous legal requirements of verification is the hallmark of professional banking. By strictly adhering to statutory frameworks, maintaining robust internal controls, and respecting the customer's mandate, the paying banker mitigates risk and upholds the integrity of negotiable instruments in commerce.
22.exam_angle: Examiners frequently test this topic through practical problem-based questions involving forged signatures, material alterations, or disregarded stop-payment orders. To score top marks, you must systematically link the factual scenario to the relevant statutory sections (Sections 31, 85, 89) and explicitly discuss whether the bank acted with 'reasonable care and good faith' to claim statutory immunity.

Wrongful dishonour creates liability for damages under Section 31.
Forgery of drawer signature means no valid discharge; bank bears the loss.
Section 85 protects bankers paying order cheques with regular endorsements.
Section 89 protects bankers against non-apparent material alterations.
A stop-payment order instantly revokes the banker's authority to pay.

23.topic: Statutory protection granted to paying bankers
23.lecture_title: Statutory Protection Granted to Paying Bankers under the Negotiable Instruments Act
23.memory_hook: Think of the paying banker as a nightclub bouncer checking IDs in the dark: if they check the ID in good faith and without negligence, the law shields them even if the ID turns out to be a brilliant fake.
23.concept_explanation:
At common law, a banker is under a strict contractual obligation to honor a customer's cheque, provided there are sufficient funds and the mandate is clear. However, the banker faces a daily operational nightmare: how can a bank teller spot every forged signature, altered amount, or unauthorized endorsement on hundreds of cheques passing through the clearinghouse? If the bank pays on a forged drawer's signature, common law says it pays out of its own money and cannot debit the customer's account. This would paralyze modern commerce.

To rescue banks from this impossible trap, the Indian Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, carves out specific statutory shields. These provisions protect the paying banker who acts in 'due course'—meaning in good faith, without negligence, and in accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument. The rationale is commercial expediency: banks are conduits of trade, not forensic handwriting experts. If a bank follows standard banking practice and processing routines without any red flags, the legislature steps in to absorb the shock of fraud, shifting the loss or providing a defense.

It is vital to distinguish between a forged drawer's signature and a forged endorsement. When a customer's own signature is forged, the banker generally cannot debit the account unless the customer's own negligence facilitated the fraud. But when a cheque is payable to order and bears a forged endorsement, the statutory provisions grant explicit immunity to the banker who pays it in due course. Understanding this boundary is the absolute core of banking operations and exam questions alike.
key_provisions: Section 10 — Defines 'Payment in Due Course' as payment in accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument, in good faith and without negligence to a person in possession under circumstances that do not afford a reasonable ground for believing that he is not entitled to receive payment.
Section 85(1) — Protects a banker paying an order cheque where the endorsement is forged, treating payment to the holder as a valid discharge of the instrument.
Section 85(2) — Protects a banker paying a bearer cheque, stating that payment to the bearer discharges the bank even if the bearer's title is defective.
Section 128 — Protects a banker paying a crossed cheque in due course in accordance with the crossing directions, granting the same protection as if payment had been made to the true owner.

case_laws.case_name: Babu Lal v. Sethiaji
case_laws.facts: A dispute arose regarding payments made on negotiable instruments where the collecting and paying banks claimed protection under statutory provisions after a fraud was uncovered in the transaction chain.
case_laws.holding: The court held that statutory protection is not a blanket immunity; it is strictly conditional upon the absence of negligence and the presence of good faith.
case_laws.why_it_matters: It established that a bank cannot simply act mechanically and claim protection; standard operating procedures and reasonable care must be demonstrably exercised.

case_laws.case_name: Commrs. of State Taxation v. Bank of New South Wales
case_laws.facts: A bank paid out on instruments bearing irregularities that should have alerted a prudent teller, leading to a suit by the true owner of the funds.
case_laws.holding: It was held that if a banker ignores glaring abnormalities on the face of the instrument, they fail the test of acting without negligence and lose statutory protection.
case_laws.why_it_matters: Reinforces the objective standard of a reasonable banker when evaluating apparent tenor and potential red flags.

23.real_world_example: In a corporate fraud scenario, an internal accountant managed to intercept incoming cheques, forge the endorsement of the payee company, and deposit them into a parallel dummy account opened at the same bank. When the payee company discovered millions missing, they sued the bank for conversion. The bank successfully relied on statutory protections under Section 85 because the tellers had processed the cheques through standard clearing channels without any glaring discrepancies on the face of the instruments that would have triggered a mandatory fraud alert.
23.illustration: Customer A draws a cheque for Rs. 50,000 payable to B or order. The cheque is stolen en route by X, who forges B's endorsement and presents it across the counter. The bank teller checks the apparent tenor, verifies that the signature of Customer A matches the specimen card, and sees a signature matching the name 'B' on the back. The teller pays X in cash. When A's statement arrives, A sues the bank. Under Section 85(1), the bank is protected because it paid in due course upon a regular apparent endorsement, even though the endorsement was forged by X.
23.quick_answer: Statutory protection for a paying banker refers to the legal shields provided under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which absolve a bank from liability when it honors a cheque in good faith and without negligence. Key provisions include Section 10 (Payment in Due Course), Section 85 (protection when paying order and bearer cheques), and Section 128 (protection for crossed cheques). To claim these protections, the banker must prove two things: first, that the payment adhered strictly to the apparent tenor of the instrument; and second, that there was a total absence of negligence, meaning no suspicious circumstances or glaring alterations were ignored. If these conditions are met, the bank is discharged from liability even if the instrument suffers from latent defects like a forged endorsement.
23.essay_answer:
Introduction: The relationship between a banker and customer is fundamentally contractual, anchored by the mandate to honor cheques. However, the sheer volume of daily commercial transactions makes absolute perfection impossible. To balance the commercial necessity of swift payment processing with the safety of customer funds, the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, incorporates statutory protections for paying bankers. These provisions shield banks from liability under specific, regulated conditions, forming a cornerstone of modern banking law.

Concept of Payment in Due Course (Section 10): The gateway to all statutory protection is Section 10, which defines 'payment in due course'. For a payment to qualify, it must satisfy three cumulative tests: it must be made in accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument, in good faith, and without negligence. Good faith implies an honest intent, while the absence of negligence requires that the banker acts as a reasonable business entity, heeding any warning signs or alterations on the face of the cheque. If a bank pays a blatantly mutilated or materially altered cheque, it shatters the umbrella of Section 10.

Statutory Shields Under Sections 85 and 128: Section 85(1) provides immense relief regarding order cheques. If a cheque is payable to order and is endorsed by or on behalf of the payee, the banker is discharged by payment in due course, even if the endorsement turns out to be a forgery. This recognizes the commercial reality that banks cannot verify every remote endorsement. Similarly, Section 85(2) protects payments made on bearer cheques. Furthermore, Section 128 extends this protection to crossed cheques, ensuring that when a banker pays a crossed cheque in accordance with the crossing instructions and in due course, they stand in the same position as if payment had been made to the true owner.

Limits of Protection and Burden of Proof: These protections are not absolute. The burden of proof lies heavily on the banker to establish that they acted without negligence. Case law consistently demonstrates that ignoring clear alterations, mismatched endorsements, or unusual presentation patterns strips the bank of its statutory immunity. If negligence is proved, the bank must bear the loss.

Conclusion: The statutory protections granted to paying bankers are vital policy instruments designed to grease the wheels of commerce. By shifting the risk away from financial intermediaries who process instruments mechanically, the law ensures efficient banking operations, provided the institution maintains basic standards of diligence and good faith.
23.exam_angle: This topic is a favorite for direct essay questions or problem-based scenarios where a cheque with a forged endorsement or alteration is paid by a bank. Examiners test whether you can link Section 10 with Section 85 and correctly apply the 'absence of negligence' test. A top-tier answer explicitly distinguishes between forged drawer signatures and forged endorsements.
quick_recap: Paying bankers face strict contractual duties overridden by statutory shields for commercial survival.
Section 10 defines payment in due course: apparent tenor, good faith, no negligence.
Section 85(1) protects banks paying order cheques with forged endorsements.
Section 128 protects banks paying crossed cheques according to instructions.
The burden of proof to show absence of negligence always rests on the bank.
